dedupe_keys.name: flood adaptation in the design of the copenhagen metro metroselskabet lines m1 to m4

description: This Climate-ADAPT case study describes how Metroselskabet, the Copenhagen metro company owned by the City of Copenhagen, the Danish state and Frederiksberg, has built flood protection into metro design since the first line was planned in the mid-1990s. For each station the highest water level from cloudbursts and storm surges was estimated, first for a 1-in-2,000-year event, which fixed the elevation of entrances, stairs, ventilation, ramps, shafts, lifts and the control centre. For the City Ring (M3, 15.5 km and 17 stations, opened 2019) and the M4 extensions to Nordhavn and Sydhavn, updated projections led to station levels three to five metres up to guard fixed installations against a 1-in-10,000-year flood. Other measures include raised steps at entrances, drainage grates and pumps at tunnel portals, pumping in all underground stations, floodgates towards other rail systems, backflow protection and waterproof doors. The City Ring cost DKK 22.4 billion (about EUR 3 billion), with adaptation costs not separated. The page, first published in 2016 and updated in 2026, is accessible online as free HTML with links to Danish climate adaptation pages. Caveats: station-level water levels and models are not published, and fixed technical requirements limited some measures. The case illustrates design for flood hazard and sea level rise in urban rail; related records are the Kujala public transport networks of 25 cities and the Mobility Database.
name: Flood adaptation in the design of the Copenhagen metro (Metroselskabet, lines M1 to M4)
outcomes: Lines M1 and M2 are now fully protected against cloudburst flooding, and City Ring and M4 stations were set three to five metres higher to protect fixed installations against a 1-in-10,000-year flood.
provider: Climate-ADAPT (European Environment Agency), case study from Metroselskabet
